fields.Front: Define 'dogma' as used in Chapter 1.
fields.Back: A set of beliefs presented as obligatory principles by the Church.

fields.Front: In the 18th century, which science challenged orthodox religion, and what concept made it a threat?
fields.Back: Geology (not astronomy or physics); it introduced the concept of evolution, i.e. the process of change. It was also the key that advanced 19th-century biology, including Darwin.

fields.Front: Who was Nicolaus Steno?
fields.Back: Danish natural philosopher (born Niels Stensen, 1638-1686); one of the first to try to understand Earth's surface from present processes; recognized the marine origin of fossils in Italy; 'father of stratigraphy'.

fields.Front: What question did Steno set out to answer?
fields.Back: 'In what way the present condition of anything discloses the past condition of that same thing.'

fields.Front: What mistake did Steno make about Earth's original surface?
fields.Back: He assumed it was a smooth pile of sediments; the early hard surface was really igneous rock.

fields.Front: What is stratigraphy?
fields.Back: The study of the layers of rocks and sediments.

fields.Text: In {{c1::1667}}, after years of heavy persuasion, Steno converted to {{c2::Roman Catholicism}} and ceased all geological work.
fields.Extra: After years of heavy persuasion he converted to Roman Catholicism and ceased all geological work.

fields.Text: Steno is called the father of {{c1::stratigraphy}}, while Hutton gets the label father of {{c2::modern geology}}.
{{c1::Thomas Burnet}}, an Anglican clergyman and confessor to King {{c2::William III}}, attributed all uneven surface features to {{c3::Noah's flood}} (water from inside Earth).
fields.Extra: An Anglican clergyman, confessor to King William III; assumed a literal biblical creation and that all uneven surface features resulted from Noah's flood, whose water came from inside Earth and returned there.

fields.Front: Why was Burnet praised and Steno ignored in their day?
fields.Back: Steno published a thin text in Latin; Burnet published 4 volumes in English. Newton and virtually all clergy praised Burnet. (Burnet was later dismissed by King William for an allegorical interpretation of creation.)

fields.Text: In {{c1::1650}} Archbishop {{c2::James Ussher}} dated Earth's creation to sunset on October 22nd, {{c3::4004 B.C.}}
fields.Extra: In 1650: Earth came into existence at sunset on October 22nd, 4004 B.C. (Earth about 6000 years old; by the slides, 5654 years old in 1650).

fields.Front: How does the reading judge Ussher's work?
fields.Back: He was 'no kook'; it is virtually impossible to fault his method - he simply had too few scientific facts. His date became dogma for over 200 years.

fields.Front: Define catastrophism as a philosophy (origin).
fields.Back: An attempt to recognize the importance of geological processes but sequence and confine them within the concept of biblical studies.

fields.Front: Who was Baron Georges Cuvier?
fields.Back: 1769-1832; head of the Paris Academy of Science, related to royalty, hugely influential, brilliant, charismatic and very rich; the leading proponent of catastrophism.

fields.Front: What did Cuvier observe in the Paris Basin and how did he interpret it?
fields.Back: Repeated layers of boulders above fine-grained sands; interpreted as repeated sudden floods caused by huge catastrophes that were sudden, violent, overwhelming and completely unpredictable; the last was Noah's flood.

fields.Text: Cuvier placed Creation {{c1::6000}} years in the past, neatly fitting {{c2::Ussher}}'s chronology.
fields.Extra: 6000 years in the past, fitting Ussher's chronology.

fields.Front: What three things did a catastrophist believe (general beliefs)?
fields.Back: Earth's history is a record of unique events; there is no natural evolution of anything, biological or inorganic; there is no possible prediction of nature.

fields.Front: EXAM DEFINITION: list the five geological assumptions of catastrophists.
fields.Back: 1) Earth began as a molten ball; 2) as it cooled it underwent intermittent global convulsions that threw rocks into mountains (even those with marine fossils); 3) valleys are the erosional signature of Noah's world-wide flood; 4) fossils are previous life forms killed off in episodic catastrophes; 5) no biological connections between species - all independent creations.

fields.Text: Catastrophists assumed Earth began as a {{c1::molten ball}}, that valleys were eroded by {{c2::Noah's flood}}, and that all species were {{c3::independent creations}} with no biological connections.

fields.Front: What was a side effect of catastrophism for the profession of science?
fields.Back: Science was a pretty useless profession; scientists called themselves 'philosophers' or 'doctors'.

fields.Front: What did Cuvier conclude from comparing mastodon and elephant bones?
fields.Back: Their remarkable similarity made evolution the easy solution, but he rejected it as neither morally correct nor within religious dogma - he 'never lost faith'.

fields.Text: Uniformitarianism was originally called {{c1::gradualism}}; the first to formulate and name it was {{c2::James Hutton}}.

fields.Front: Who first recognized the concept of gradualism but did not name or develop it?
fields.Back: Leonardo da Vinci; Steno then applied it intuitively in the mid-to-late 1600s without naming it.

fields.Text: {{c1::James Hutton}} (1726-1797) first formulated and named gradualism in his {{c2::1795}} book '{{c3::Theory of Geology}}', two years before his death.
fields.Extra: James Hutton (1726-1797), in his 1795 book the reading calls 'Theory of Geology', two years before his death.

fields.Text: A {{c1::deist}} believes in a deity but not in divine intervention or conformity of nature to scripture; {{c2::Hutton}} and {{c3::Lyell}} were deists.
fields.Extra: One who believes in a deity but not in divine intervention or in conformity of natural processes to scripture; Hutton and Lyell.

fields.Front: What did Hutton observe that led to gradualism?
fields.Back: Streams eroding sand and depositing it in quieter water; he concluded the same process formed ancient sandstones and that great time was required (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition, solidification).

fields.Front: Why did Hutton's ideas fail to compete during his lifetime?
fields.Back: He was cautious, used words sparingly and was not an eloquent speaker, whereas Cuvier was eloquent and dynamic.

fields.Front: Who was Charles Lyell?
fields.Back: 1797-1875; wealthy Scot, trained as a lawyer at Oxford, switched to geology after one lecture; Professor of Geology at King's College (early 1830s); brilliant, popular (and nasty) speaker who promoted uniformitarianism.

fields.Text: {{c1::Charles Lyell}} wrote '{{c2::Principles of Geology}}' in {{c3::1830}}, championing Hutton and emphasizing unlimited geological time.
fields.Extra: 'Principles of Geology' (1830), championing Hutton's hypotheses and emphasizing unlimited geological time.

fields.Front: Why did Lyell 'carry the day' for uniformitarianism?
fields.Back: Cuvier died in 1832 and there was no vociferous successor in the catastrophist camp; Lyell's eloquence changed the whole philosophy of Earth Science.

fields.Front: State the Law of Uniformitarianism and its meaning.
fields.Back: 'The present is the key to the past': the processes we observe today always did operate and will continue to operate at similar rates.

fields.Text: The Law of Uniformitarianism: '{{c1::the present is the key to the past}}'.
Hutton published in {{c1::1795}}; Lyell's 'Principles of Geology' appeared in {{c2::1830}}; Cuvier died in {{c3::1832}}.
Meteor (Barringer) Crater, {{c1::1 km}} across in the {{c2::Arizona}} desert, was kept off the state map until {{c3::1960}} - uniformitarianism taken to extremes.
fields.Extra: A 1 km diameter asteroid impact crater in Arizona (Barringer Crater) was kept off the map of Arizona until 1960 because 'everyone knew that large rocks did not fall from the skies'.

fields.Text: At the 65.5 Ma horizon {{c1::65-70%}} of species vanish; the crater is at least {{c2::180 km}} across, from an asteroid {{c3::10-12 km}} in diameter - yet some still deny the impact.
fields.Extra: A knife-sharp horizon where 65-70% of species vanish (most dinosaurs), a crater at least 180 km across from a 10-12 km asteroid, global forest fires and tsunami over 1 km high - yet dozens of articles still deny the impact or its importance.

fields.Front: What lesson does Chapter 1 draw from the catastrophism vs uniformitarianism 'war'?
fields.Back: It damaged scientific advancement for centuries; deeply held philosophies can be dangerous to the learning process.

fields.Front: According to the slides, what theory ended the dominance of uniformitarianism?
fields.Back: Plate tectonics.
